topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Forward model
topics.description: A deterministic rule that turns a set of Earth-model parameters (for example fault slip) into the data they would produce (for example GNSS displacements). Running it is the forward direction; inversion asks the question backwards.
evidence: State the inputs (parameters) and outputs (predicted data) of a given forward model
Explain why running the same forward model twice gives the same prediction
topics.assessmentPrompt: For a buried fault and three GNSS stations, can you say what goes into the forward model and what comes out?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Measurement noise
topics.description: The random difference between what an instrument records and what the Earth actually did, described by a probability distribution with a typical size σ.
evidence: Describe noise by its typical size σ and its distribution
Explain why repeated measurements of the same displacement differ
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a station's noise has σ = 2 mm, roughly how far from the true value do you expect most readings to be?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Going backwards: the inverse problem
topics.description: Using data and a forward model to say which parameter values are consistent with the observations. With noise, the answer is a set of acceptable models with weights, not a single model.
evidence: Explain why one noisy datum is consistent with many parameter values
Sketch the set of models that fit one station's datum within the noise
topics.assessmentPrompt: With one station and two unknowns, why can't the data alone pick a single answer?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Prior
topics.description: A probability distribution describing what is believed about the parameters before seeing the data: physical bounds, typical sizes, smoothness.
evidence: Name the kinds of information a prior can carry (sign, size, smoothness)
Explain why the answer depends on the prior when the data are weak
topics.assessmentPrompt: Before any data, what would you write down about the slip on a fault you know is a thrust?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Likelihood
topics.description: How probable the observed data are for a given set of parameters, computed from the forward model's prediction and the noise distribution. Read as a function of the parameters, it scores how well each candidate fits.
evidence: Compare the likelihood of one datum under two candidate models with Gaussian noise
Explain why the likelihood is not a probability distribution over the parameters
topics.assessmentPrompt: Two candidates predict 10 mm and 14 mm; the station recorded 11 mm with σ = 2 mm. Which has the higher likelihood?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Posterior
topics.description: The belief about the parameters after seeing the data: proportional to the prior times the likelihood.
evidence: State that the posterior is proportional to prior × likelihood
Explain why the posterior is narrower than the prior when the data are informative
topics.assessmentPrompt: If the prior and the likelihood both favour the same value, what happens to the width of the posterior?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: A posterior as a crowd of possible Earths
topics.description: A posterior can be represented by many sampled models, each a complete deterministic Earth that fits the data within the noise; dense parts of the crowd are the probable ones.
evidence: Explain what one sample from a posterior represents
Read a histogram of samples as an approximation to the posterior density
topics.assessmentPrompt: If 900 of 1,000 samples have slip between 1 and 2 m, what does that say about the slip?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: The shape of a posterior
topics.description: How the probability is spread over parameter space: one round peak, a tilted ridge, a curved banana, several separated peaks, or a flat direction the data cannot see. The shape decides which computing method works.
evidence: Recognise round, ridge, banana, multi-peak and flat shapes in a 2-D plot
Say which shape two strongly correlated parameters produce
topics.assessmentPrompt: What would the posterior look like if two parameters could trade off against each other perfectly?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: True value versus reference posterior
topics.description: In a synthetic test the true value is the parameter that generated the data; the reference posterior is the correct Bayesian answer for those noisy data. Methods are graded against the reference posterior, which need not be centred on the true value.
evidence: Explain why a correct posterior can miss the true value
Say which of the two a sampler should be graded against
topics.assessmentPrompt: Your sampler's 90 % region misses the true value in one synthetic test. Is the sampler wrong?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Model error: the forward model is not the Earth
topics.description: The difference between what the real Earth would produce and what the forward model predicts, for example from a simplified elastic structure or fault geometry. Unlike noise, it does not average out with more data.
evidence: Distinguish model error from measurement noise
Explain why adding more data does not remove model error
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you doubled the number of stations, which of the two errors would shrink?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Credible region
topics.description: A region of parameter space holding a stated posterior probability, such as 90 %, given the data and the model. A highest-density region is the smallest such region.
evidence: State what a 90 % credible region does and does not promise
Distinguish a credible region from a highest-density region
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does a 90 % credible region contain the true value 90 % of the time for every true value?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Coverage
topics.description: The share of repeated synthetic tests in which a region contains the true value. Averaged over true values drawn from the prior, 90 % credible regions cover 90 % of the time; at one fixed true value the share can differ greatly.
evidence: Run a coverage test over repeated synthetic data
Explain why fixed-truth coverage can be far from nominal
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why can a correct Bayesian 90 % interval cover a fixed true value only a quarter of the time?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Why samplers: grids do not scale
topics.description: Evaluating a posterior on a grid needs (points per axis) to the power (number of unknowns) forward runs, impossible beyond a few unknowns; samplers draw a crowd of models instead.
evidence: Estimate the grid cost for a given number of unknowns
Explain what a sampler produces instead of a grid
topics.assessmentPrompt: How many forward runs would a grid of 100 points per axis need for 10 unknowns?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Bayes' rule as multiplying two curves
topics.description: In one dimension the posterior is the prior curve times the likelihood curve, rescaled to unit area; it sits between them, closer to the narrower one.
evidence: Sketch prior, likelihood and posterior for one unknown
Predict where the posterior peak falls between the prior and likelihood peaks
topics.assessmentPrompt: If the likelihood is much narrower than the prior, where does the posterior peak?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Each datum is a band in parameter space
topics.description: With two unknowns, one datum is consistent with a band of parameter pairs; the posterior is where the bands of all data (and the prior) overlap.
evidence: Draw the band one datum allows
Explain how a second datum with a different slope narrows the posterior
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why do two stations that see the fault from the same direction constrain it poorly?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: When the posterior is exactly Gaussian
topics.description: A linear forward model with a Gaussian prior and Gaussian noise gives an exactly Gaussian posterior, fully described by a mean and a covariance; a nonlinear forward model generally does not.
evidence: List the three conditions for an exactly Gaussian posterior
Give an example where a nonlinear forward model bends the posterior
topics.assessmentPrompt: Which of the three conditions fails for an earthquake location from travel times?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Trade-offs between parameters
topics.description: When two parameters can change together without changing the predictions much, the posterior is a long tilted ridge: each is poorly known on its own, their combination well known. Locking depth and slip rate of a strike-slip fault are a classic pair.
evidence: Recognise a trade-off as a tilted ridge
Explain why a well-determined combination can hide two poorly determined parameters
topics.assessmentPrompt: If locking depth and slip rate trade off, what can the data still tell you?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: The funnel
topics.description: A posterior shape where one parameter (a scale) controls the spread of others: wide at one end, narrow at the other. Common in hierarchical models and hard for samplers that use one step size.
evidence: Recognise a funnel in a 2-D plot of a scale and a parameter
Name the kind of model that produces funnels
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why does a funnel need small steps in one region and large steps in another?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Gaussian, flat and smooth: three words
topics.description: 'Gaussian' describes a posterior's shape; 'flat' a direction along which the density does not change (a flat prior, or a direction the data cannot see); 'smooth' either a solution whose neighbouring values are correlated or a log posterior that is differentiable.
evidence: Use each of the three words correctly
Tell the two meanings of 'smooth' apart
topics.assessmentPrompt: Is a 'smooth slip model' the same thing as a 'smooth log posterior'?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: The zoo of test shapes
topics.description: Six two-parameter test posteriors with known answers (round Gaussian, correlated ridge, flat ridge, banana, two modes, funnel), used to grade every method in the course.
evidence: Name the six test shapes
Say which difficulty each shape tests
topics.assessmentPrompt: Which test shape would expose a sampler that gets stuck in one mode?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Random variable, pdf and cdf
topics.description: A quantity whose value is uncertain, described by a probability density function (pdf: where values are likely) or a cumulative distribution function (cdf: the probability of falling below a threshold).
evidence: Read a probability from a pdf as an area
Read the same probability directly from a cdf
topics.assessmentPrompt: How do you get the probability that x lies between 1 and 2 from the pdf, and from the cdf?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Expectation (mean)
topics.description: The probability-weighted average of a random variable: the balance point of its distribution.
evidence: Compute a mean from samples and from a simple pdf
Explain why one large outlier can move the mean far
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why can the mean of a skewed distribution lie where few values occur?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Variance and standard deviation
topics.description: Variance is the expected squared distance from the mean; its square root, the standard deviation σ, is the typical spread in the units of the quantity.
evidence: Compute variance and σ from samples
Explain why σ, not the variance, is quoted as an error bar
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a set of readings has variance 4 mm², what is their standard deviation?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Quantiles, median and mode
topics.description: A quantile is the value below which a given share of the probability lies; the median is the 50 % quantile and the mode the most probable value. For skewed distributions mean, median and mode differ.
evidence: Read the 5 %, 50 % and 95 % quantiles from a cdf
Say when mean, median and mode coincide
topics.assessmentPrompt: For a distribution with a long right tail, which is larger: the mean or the median?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: The Gaussian (normal) distribution
topics.description: The bell-shaped distribution set by a mean and a standard deviation; about 68 % of the probability lies within one σ of the mean and about 95 % within two.
evidence: Write the Gaussian density
Use the one-σ and two-σ rules of thumb
topics.assessmentPrompt: Roughly what share of Gaussian errors fall outside 2σ?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Heavy tails
topics.description: Distributions such as the Laplace and the Student-t put much more probability far from the centre than a Gaussian with the same spread, so large values (outliers) are much less surprising.
evidence: Compare the tail probabilities of Gaussian, Laplace and Student-t
Explain why a Gaussian noise model is fragile to outliers
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why does one outlier pull a least-squares fit more than a Student-t fit?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Chi-square: checking that σ is right
topics.description: The sum of squared residuals in units of σ. For N independent Gaussian residuals with the right σ it averages N, so χ²/N is near 1; much larger means σ is too small or the model misfits, much smaller means σ is too large.
evidence: Compute χ² and χ²/N from residuals and σ
Interpret χ²/N far above and far below 1
topics.assessmentPrompt: Your fit gives χ²/N = 0.1. What does that suggest about your σ?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Covariance and correlation
topics.description: Covariance measures how two quantities vary together: positive when they rise together, negative when one rises as the other falls. Correlation is the covariance scaled to lie between −1 and 1. A covariance matrix holds variances on its diagonal and covariances off it.
evidence: Compute a covariance and a correlation from paired samples
Read the sign and strength of a correlation from a scatter plot
topics.assessmentPrompt: Two stations share a common-mode error. Is the covariance of their errors positive or negative?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: The multivariate Gaussian and its ellipses
topics.description: A Gaussian for several quantities at once, set by a mean vector and a covariance matrix; its contours are ellipses whose axes and tilt come from the covariance.
evidence: Draw a 2-D Gaussian ellipse from a covariance matrix
Explain what a tilted ellipse says about two parameters
topics.assessmentPrompt: What does a circular ellipse imply about the covariance matrix?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a covariance
topics.description: The eigenvectors of a covariance matrix are the axes of its ellipse and the eigenvalues are the variances along those axes.
evidence: Draw an ellipse's axes from an eigen-decomposition
Explain what a near-zero eigenvalue means
topics.assessmentPrompt: If the smallest eigenvalue of a posterior covariance is tiny, what does that say about that direction?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Positive definiteness: when a covariance is valid
topics.description: A valid covariance gives every weighted combination aᵀCa a variance that is not negative (positive semi-definite); it is positive definite when no combination is exactly fixed. It fails for perfectly correlated quantities, sum-to-one constraints, ensembles with fewer members than unknowns, smoothing operators with a null space, impossible hand-built matrices, and through round-off.
evidence: Test positive definiteness from eigenvalues
Name three ways a covariance becomes singular
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why is the sample covariance of 5 draws of 10 quantities singular?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: The log-normal distribution
topics.description: A positive quantity whose logarithm is Gaussian; natural for quantities known to an order of magnitude, such as viscosity.
evidence: Generate log-normal draws from Gaussian ones
Explain why the log-normal is skewed
topics.assessmentPrompt: If ln η is Gaussian with mean ln(10¹⁹), what is the median of η?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Joint, marginal and conditional
topics.description: The joint distribution describes two quantities together; a marginal is the distribution of one, summed over the other; a conditional is the distribution of one given a value of the other, a slice of the joint rescaled to unit area.
evidence: Compute a marginal and a conditional from a joint table
Explain why the posterior is a conditional distribution
topics.assessmentPrompt: Is p(slip | data) a marginal or a conditional?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Independence
topics.description: Two quantities are independent when knowing one says nothing about the other: their joint distribution is the product of the marginals.
evidence: Test independence from a joint table
Give an example of dependent measurement errors
topics.assessmentPrompt: If two stations' errors share a common-mode term, are they independent?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Uncorrelated is not independent
topics.description: Zero correlation only rules out a straight-line relation; quantities can depend strongly on each other and still be uncorrelated (x and x² for symmetric x). For jointly Gaussian quantities the two coincide.
evidence: Construct an uncorrelated but dependent pair
State when zero correlation does imply independence
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can x and x² be uncorrelated?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Bayes' rule, derived
topics.description: From the product rule, p(a, b) = p(a | b) p(b) = p(b | a) p(a), follows p(m | d) = p(d | m) p(m) / p(d). The denominator only normalises the posterior.
evidence: Derive Bayes' rule from the product rule
Explain why p(d) can be ignored when sampling
topics.assessmentPrompt: What role does p(d) play when you only want the shape of the posterior?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Conditioning a joint Gaussian
topics.description: For jointly Gaussian parameters and data, the parameters given the data are Gaussian, with the mean shifted by a gain times the misfit and a reduced covariance: the Kalman update in its simplest form.
evidence: Apply the conditioning formula in two dimensions
Explain how the update reaches a parameter that was not observed
topics.assessmentPrompt: If two parameters are correlated in the prior and you observe only one, does the other change?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: The Kalman gain
topics.description: The matrix that says how much of the data misfit to add to each parameter: large when the data are precise relative to the prior, small when they are noisy. It returns in linear inversion (2.08), filtering (2.23) and ensemble methods (2.24).
evidence: Compute the gain for one parameter and one datum
Explain the gain as a trust ratio between prior and data
topics.assessmentPrompt: What happens to the gain as the data noise goes to zero?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Law of large numbers
topics.description: The average of many independent draws settles toward the expectation as the number of draws grows.
evidence: Demonstrate a sample mean settling down
State what the law does not say about how fast
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why does a mean from 10 draws fluctuate more than one from 10,000?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Monte Carlo error and the standard error
topics.description: The uncertainty of an average of N draws: for independent draws it is σ/√N, the standard error. Correlated draws carry less information.
evidence: Compute the standard error of a sample mean
Explain why correlated draws inflate the Monte Carlo error
topics.assessmentPrompt: How many more independent draws do you need to halve the standard error?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Effective sample size
topics.description: The number of independent draws that would give the same Monte Carlo error as a set of correlated draws; for a Markov chain it can be far smaller than the number of draws.
evidence: Explain the effective sample size in words
Say how it changes with autocorrelation
topics.assessmentPrompt: A chain of 10,000 draws has an effective sample size of 100. How precise is its mean compared with 10,000 independent draws?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Central limit theorem
topics.description: Sums of many independent small contributions tend to a Gaussian whatever their individual distributions, provided the variance is finite; this is why so much noise looks Gaussian.
evidence: Show a sum of uniform draws becoming Gaussian
State the finite-variance condition
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why might noise that is the sum of many small effects look Gaussian?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: When averaging fails: infinite variance
topics.description: For distributions without a finite variance, such as the Cauchy, averages do not settle and the central limit theorem does not apply.
evidence: Show a Cauchy sample mean that does not converge
Link this failure to robust losses
topics.assessmentPrompt: Would averaging more readings help if the errors were Cauchy-distributed?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Coloured noise: when √N is too optimistic
topics.description: When successive errors are correlated in time (flicker or random-walk noise), the error of an average or a rate shrinks more slowly than 1/√N, so white-noise error bars are too small.
evidence: Compare averaging white and correlated noise
Explain why a long GNSS series can still give an uncertain rate
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why can doubling a GNSS series' length help less than expected?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Bernstein-von Mises: posteriors become Gaussian
topics.description: With enough informative data, a well-behaved posterior approaches a Gaussian centred near the maximum-likelihood value, and the prior's influence fades.
evidence: Show a posterior narrowing and becoming Gaussian as data grow
State when the result does not apply (non-identifiable or bounded parameters)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why does a posterior with a hard bound at the true value not become Gaussian?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Notation, shapes and units
topics.description: Scalars in italic, vectors in bold lower case, matrices in bold upper case; every matrix has a shape (rows × columns) and units, and checking both catches most algebra mistakes.
evidence: Give the shape and units of G, m, d and C_d in a slip inversion
Check an expression by its shapes
topics.assessmentPrompt: If d has 30 entries and m has 12, what is the shape of G?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: A linear forward model as d = G m
topics.description: For a linear problem the prediction is a matrix-vector product: each column of G is the data produced by one unit of one parameter (a Green's function), and d adds the columns weighted by the parameters.
evidence: Read a column of G as the response to one parameter
Compute d = G m for a small example
topics.assessmentPrompt: What does the third column of G represent?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: The transpose: data back to parameters
topics.description: Gᵀ maps data-space vectors back to parameter space; Gᵀr collects, for each parameter, how much the residuals point along its Green's function. It is the gradient of a least-squares misfit and the core of every adjoint.
evidence: Compute Gᵀr for a small residual
Explain Gᵀr as the gradient of a squared misfit
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why is Gᵀ, not G⁻¹, what turns residuals into a direction in parameter space?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Inverse and determinant
topics.description: The inverse undoes a square matrix; the determinant measures how it scales areas or volumes, and is zero exactly when the matrix squashes some direction flat and has no inverse.
evidence: Compute a 2 × 2 inverse and determinant
Relate a zero determinant to a lost direction
topics.assessmentPrompt: What does a zero determinant say about a square forward model?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: The Cholesky factorisation
topics.description: Writing a positive-definite covariance as C = L Lᵀ with L lower-triangular, a square root of C. It turns independent draws into correlated ones (x = L z), solves systems with two triangular solves, and gives the log-determinant; it fails when a pivot becomes zero or negative.
evidence: Generate correlated noise with x = L z
Explain why Cholesky fails on a matrix that is not positive definite, and what a small jitter does
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why does adding a tiny value to the diagonal let a failing Cholesky finish?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Whitening
topics.description: Transforming correlated residuals with L⁻¹ so they become independent with unit variance; χ² with a full covariance is the sum of squares of the whitened residuals.
evidence: Whiten residuals with a Cholesky factor
Compute χ² with a full data covariance
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why does the same residual give a different χ² with and without the off-diagonal covariances?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Solve, do not invert
topics.description: Forming A⁻¹ explicitly loses accuracy and time; solving with a factorisation (Cholesky, QR, SVD) is more stable, and forming GᵀG squares the condition number.
evidence: Explain the condition number in words
Choose a stable solver for a least-squares problem
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why can forming GᵀG lose half the significant digits?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: SVD, rank and null space
topics.description: The singular value decomposition writes G as independent channels, each a parameter pattern mapped to a data pattern with a gain (a singular value). The rank counts the nonzero gains; patterns with zero gain form the null space, invisible to the data.
evidence: Read the rank and the null space from the singular values
Construct two models that predict identical data
topics.assessmentPrompt: With 3 stations and 5 unknowns, how many independent slip patterns, at least, are invisible to the data?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: The log-determinant
topics.description: The Gaussian likelihood needs log det C; computing it as twice the sum of the logs of the Cholesky diagonal (or with slogdet) avoids the overflow and underflow of det itself.
evidence: Compute log det C from a Cholesky factor
Explain why det C overflows for a large C
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why does log(det(C)) fail for a 1,000 × 1,000 covariance?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Least squares and the normal equations
topics.description: The model that minimises the sum of squared residuals; for d = G m it solves the normal equations GᵀG m = Gᵀd.
evidence: Fit a straight line by least squares by hand
Derive the normal equations from the misfit
topics.assessmentPrompt: Which equation does setting the gradient of ‖d − G m‖² to zero give?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Least squares is maximum likelihood
topics.description: With independent Gaussian noise of equal σ, maximising the likelihood is the same as minimising the sum of squared residuals.
evidence: Show that minus the log likelihood is ½χ² plus a constant
Say which noise assumption least squares hides
topics.assessmentPrompt: Which noise model do you assume when you use least squares?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Weighted least squares with C_d
topics.description: Each residual is weighted by the inverse data covariance, so precise data count more and correlated errors are not double-counted: minimise (d − G m)ᵀ C_d⁻¹ (d − G m).
evidence: Set up weighted least squares for two data sets of different precision
Explain what a diagonal C_d ignores
topics.assessmentPrompt: What happens if you give a noisy data set the same weight as a precise one?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: The Gauss-Markov theorem and its limits
topics.description: Among linear unbiased estimators, weighted least squares has the smallest variance (for a full-rank design and known noise covariance). Biased estimators, such as regularised ones, can have a smaller mean-squared error.
evidence: State the theorem's conditions
Give an example where a biased estimator has a lower error
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does the Gauss-Markov theorem say least squares beats every estimator?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: χ² as a goodness-of-fit check
topics.description: After a fit, χ²/N near one says the misfit matches the assumed noise; far above means misfit or underestimated noise, far below means overestimated noise.
evidence: Compute χ²/N after a weighted fit
Diagnose a fit with χ²/N much larger than one
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can a fit with χ²/N close to 1 still be wrong?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Ill-posed problems
topics.description: When the data cannot pin down every parameter (more unknowns than independent data, or tiny singular values), least-squares solutions are not unique or oscillate wildly: the problem needs extra information, a prior or regularisation.
evidence: Recognise an ill-posed problem from its singular values
Explain why noise is amplified along small singular values
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why does a least-squares slip model on many patches oscillate?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Resolution: each estimate is a blurred average
topics.description: Each estimated parameter is a weighted average of the true ones; the resolution matrix holds these weights, and its rows show how blurred each estimate is.
evidence: Read a row of a resolution matrix
Relate resolution to station geometry
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why is deep slip usually poorly resolved by surface data?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Combining a prior and a datum: precision weighting
topics.description: For one unknown with a Gaussian prior and one Gaussian datum, the posterior mean is the precision-weighted average of the prior mean and the datum, and the posterior precision (one over the variance) is the sum of the two precisions.
evidence: Compute the posterior mean and σ by hand
Explain why the posterior is narrower than both inputs
topics.assessmentPrompt: Prior 0 ± 2, datum 3 ± 1: is the posterior mean closer to 0 or to 3?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Bayesian linear inversion
topics.description: For d = G m plus Gaussian noise with a Gaussian prior, the posterior is Gaussian with a closed-form mean and covariance: no sampling is needed.
evidence: Write the posterior mean and covariance formulas
Compute them for a two-parameter problem
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why is no sampler needed for a linear-Gaussian inversion?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: The MAP estimate
topics.description: The maximum a posteriori estimate is the most probable parameter value; for a Gaussian prior and noise it minimises misfit plus a prior penalty, which is regularised least squares.
evidence: Write the MAP objective for a Gaussian prior
Relate the prior penalty to a regulariser
topics.assessmentPrompt: Which term in the MAP objective comes from the prior?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Model-space and data-space forms
topics.description: The same linear-Gaussian posterior can be computed with a matrix of size unknowns × unknowns or data × data; choose the smaller. The data-space form contains the Kalman gain.
evidence: Choose the cheaper form for a given problem size
Show that the two forms give the same answer
topics.assessmentPrompt: With 10,000 unknowns and 50 data, which form do you use?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Mean, median and MAP
topics.description: Different summaries answer different questions: the mean minimises the expected squared error, the median the absolute error; the MAP is the highest density and changes with the choice of coordinates. They agree only for symmetric posteriors with one peak.
evidence: Compute the mean, median and MAP of a skewed posterior
Explain why the MAP depends on the parameterisation
topics.assessmentPrompt: Which summary changes if you work with log viscosity instead of viscosity?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: The Hessian: curvature of the log posterior
topics.description: The matrix of second derivatives of minus the log posterior; at the peak it measures how sharply the posterior falls off in each direction.
evidence: Relate a large curvature to a well-determined direction
Compute the Hessian of a quadratic misfit
topics.assessmentPrompt: For a linear-Gaussian problem, how is the Hessian related to the posterior covariance?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: The Laplace approximation
topics.description: A Gaussian centred at the MAP with a covariance equal to the inverse Hessian of minus the log posterior; exact for linear-Gaussian problems, an approximation otherwise.
evidence: Build a Laplace approximation in one dimension
Show where it fails for a skewed posterior
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why can a Laplace approximation be badly wrong near a bound?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: What did the data teach each parameter?
topics.description: Comparing the posterior with the prior variance, parameter by parameter, separates what the data constrain from what the prior supplies.
evidence: Compute the posterior-to-prior variance ratio
Identify parameters dominated by the prior
topics.assessmentPrompt: A patch has a posterior σ equal to its prior σ. What did the data tell you about it?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: A regulariser is a prior
topics.description: Adding a penalty to the misfit is the same as multiplying the likelihood by a prior: minus the log prior is the penalty. The penalty's shape decides the character of the answer.
evidence: Translate an L2 penalty into a Gaussian prior
Explain the regularisation weight λ as a prior width
topics.assessmentPrompt: Which prior corresponds to the penalty λ‖m‖²?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: L2 regularisation (ridge, damping)
topics.description: Penalising the sum of squared parameters shrinks all of them smoothly toward zero; it is a Gaussian prior centred at zero.
evidence: Show the shrinkage of a least-squares estimate
Choose λ from a prior standard deviation
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does L2 regularisation ever set a parameter exactly to zero?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: L1 regularisation (lasso, sparsity)
topics.description: Penalising the sum of absolute values (a Laplace prior) sets small parameters exactly to zero in the MAP (soft-thresholding), giving sparse solutions.
evidence: Apply soft-thresholding to an estimate
Explain why L1 gives exact zeros and L2 does not
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why does an L1 MAP contain many exact zeros?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Smoothing: first- and second-difference penalties
topics.description: Penalising differences between neighbouring parameters (first differences) or their curvature (second differences, the Laplacian) favours smooth slip without pulling its level toward zero.
evidence: Build a first-difference operator
Say which patterns the penalty leaves free
topics.assessmentPrompt: Which slip pattern costs nothing under a first-difference penalty?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Total variation
topics.description: Penalising the sum of absolute differences between neighbours favours blocky, piecewise-constant models with sharp edges.
evidence: Contrast total variation with second-difference smoothing on a step
topics.assessmentPrompt: Which penalty keeps a sharp slip edge: total variation or the Laplacian?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: What a prior believes: draws before the data
topics.description: Drawing random models from a prior shows what it considers typical before seeing data; priors with similar MAPs can believe very different things.
evidence: Draw samples from a smoothing prior
Judge a prior's realism from its draws
topics.assessmentPrompt: What do draws from an L1 prior look like compared with draws from an L2 prior?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Laplacian smoothing and the Matérn prior
topics.description: A Laplacian smoothing prior is a close relative of a Matérn Gaussian-process prior, which makes its length scale and smoothness explicit.
evidence: Explain the length-scale counterpart of a smoothing weight
topics.assessmentPrompt: What does the Matérn form make explicit that a plain Laplacian penalty hides?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: A sparse MAP, a posterior that is not sparse
topics.description: The L1 MAP has exact zeros, but samples from the same posterior are not sparse: sparsity is a property of the optimum, not of the belief.
evidence: Compare an L1 MAP with posterior draws
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you report only the L1 MAP, what does it hide?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: A loss is a negative log posterior
topics.description: The objective a fitting program minimises; choosing a loss is choosing a noise model and a prior.
evidence: Write the loss for Gaussian noise and a Gaussian prior
Translate a loss back into a noise model
topics.assessmentPrompt: Which noise model does an absolute-value loss assume?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Robust losses and outliers
topics.description: Losses that grow slowly for large residuals (L1, Huber, Student-t) limit the pull of outliers; a squared loss gives every outlier a pull proportional to its size.
evidence: Compare the influence of an outlier under squared and Huber losses
Fit a GPS velocity containing outliers with a robust loss
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why does one bad GPS day move a least-squares velocity?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Judging errors in units of the data noise
topics.description: A 2 mm error is negligible for noisy data and large for precise data; residuals and surrogate errors should be judged in units of σ.
evidence: Express a prediction error in σ units
topics.assessmentPrompt: Is a 1 mm prediction error large?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: The Jacobian
topics.description: The matrix of first derivatives of every predicted datum with respect to every parameter: the local linear version of a nonlinear forward model, and G itself for a linear one.
evidence: Compute a Jacobian entry by finite differences
Explain the Jacobian as a local tangent
topics.assessmentPrompt: For a linear forward model, what is the Jacobian?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Optimisers: from gradient descent to Gauss-Newton
topics.description: Gradient descent, momentum and Adam follow the gradient; Gauss-Newton, Levenberg-Marquardt and L-BFGS also use curvature and converge in far fewer steps on smooth least-squares problems.
evidence: Run gradient descent and Gauss-Newton on the same problem
Explain why curvature information speeds convergence
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why does Gauss-Newton need far fewer iterations than gradient descent in a narrow valley?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Scaling and preconditioning
topics.description: A long tilted valley in the loss makes gradient methods zigzag; rescaling or whitening the parameters makes the valley round and the problem easy.
evidence: Compute the condition number of a Hessian
Precondition a problem by rescaling
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why does changing parameter units change how fast gradient descent converges?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Several starts, several answers
topics.description: Nonlinear losses can have several minima or flat valleys; different starting points end in different places, and a 'converged' message does not mean the global minimum.
evidence: Run several starts and compare their end points
Recognise a valley the data cannot resolve
topics.assessmentPrompt: Two starts end at different parameters with equal loss. What does that tell you?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Mini-batches and stochastic gradients
topics.description: Using a random subset of the data at each step gives a noisy but cheap gradient; the noise makes the path jitter and must be controlled with the step size.
evidence: Explain the trade-off of the batch size
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why does a batch of one datum make the parameter path jitter?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Stopping early is a regulariser
topics.description: Iterative solvers fit the well-determined parts first; stopping before convergence acts like a filter on the small singular values, so the number of iterations is a regularisation choice.
evidence: Show semi-convergence on an ill-posed problem
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why does the error first fall and then rise as the iterations continue?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: A minimum is not an uncertainty
topics.description: An optimiser returns one point; an uncertainty needs the curvature (a Laplace approximation) or a sampler, and the curvature can mislead when the posterior is not Gaussian.
evidence: Build a Laplace approximation at an optimum
Show where it fails
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why can't an optimiser's final answer alone give an error bar?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Prior families
topics.description: Gaussian, Laplace, Student-t, uniform, half-normal, truncated normal and log-normal priors encode different knowledge: a typical size, the tails, hard bounds, a sign, an order of magnitude.
evidence: Match a prior family to a statement of what is known
Compare their tail probabilities
topics.assessmentPrompt: Which family would you use for a quantity known only to an order of magnitude?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Flat is not neutral: parameterisation and the Jacobian
topics.description: A uniform prior is uniform in only one parameterisation; changing variables multiplies the density by the Jacobian |dx/dy|, so 'uniform in viscosity' and 'uniform in log viscosity' are different beliefs.
evidence: Transform a density with the Jacobian rule
Compare the probability per decade under two 'flat' priors
topics.assessmentPrompt: Uniform viscosity between 10¹⁸ and 10²¹ Pa s: which decade gets most of the probability?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: The logit transform for two-sided bounds
topics.description: The logit stretches a bounded interval onto the whole number line and its inverse, the sigmoid, maps it back, so unbounded steps (samplers, ensemble updates, optimisers, networks) never leave the bounds. A wide Gaussian in logit space piles probability against the bounds.
evidence: Map a bounded parameter to logit space and back
Include the Jacobian when writing a prior in logit space
Predict the shape of a logit-normal distribution from its spread
topics.assessmentPrompt: Is a Gaussian prior with standard deviation 3 in logit space uninformative about a fraction?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: The Dirichlet prior
topics.description: A prior for non-negative shares that sum to one, controlled by a concentration parameter: small values favour a few large shares, large values near-equal sharing.
evidence: Draw Dirichlet shares for several concentrations
Use it to share a fixed total among patches
topics.assessmentPrompt: Which concentration makes slip concentrate on a few patches?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Prior-predictive checks
topics.description: Simulate data from models drawn from the prior before fitting; if the simulated data are physically absurd or far from anything plausible, revise the prior.
evidence: Simulate data from prior draws
Revise a prior that predicts impossible totals
topics.assessmentPrompt: What share of prior draws should give a negative total slip on a fault you know is a thrust?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Where the data decide and where the prior does
topics.description: Comparing posteriors under different priors, parameter by parameter, shows which parts of the answer come from the data and which from the prior.
evidence: Compute posterior-to-prior spread ratios
Run the same inversion under two priors
topics.assessmentPrompt: Deep patches change a lot when you swap priors. What does that say?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Improper priors
topics.description: A 'prior' that does not integrate to a finite value, such as a uniform density on an infinite range. It is usable only if the data make the posterior proper, which fails along directions the data cannot see.
evidence: Recognise an improper prior
Explain when it gives an improper posterior
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why does a flat prior on unbounded slip fail when the forward model has a null space?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Gaussian process
topics.description: A Gaussian prior on a whole function: any finite set of its values is jointly Gaussian, with a covariance given by a kernel of the distance between points.
evidence: Draw functions from a Gaussian-process prior
Explain a Gaussian process as a large multivariate Gaussian
topics.assessmentPrompt: What decides how wiggly Gaussian-process draws are?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Kernels and the Matérn family
topics.description: The kernel sets the roughness: squared-exponential draws are infinitely smooth, Matérn kernels with smoothness ν range from rough (ν = 1/2) to smooth.
evidence: Compare draws for different ν
Choose a kernel for a physical field
topics.assessmentPrompt: Which kernel gives rough, kinked slip profiles?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Length scale and amplitude
topics.description: The length scale sets the distance over which values stay correlated; the amplitude sets their typical size.
evidence: Predict draws for a long and a short length scale
topics.assessmentPrompt: Halving the length scale does what to the draws?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Gaussian-process regression
topics.description: Conditioning a Gaussian-process prior on noisy observations gives a posterior mean curve and a credible band that widens away from the data.
evidence: Compute a Gaussian-process posterior from a few points
Explain why the band widens between data
topics.assessmentPrompt: What happens to the band far from all data?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: The evidence (marginal likelihood)
topics.description: The probability of the data under a model with its parameters integrated out, p(d) in Bayes' rule. It normalises the posterior and scores how well a whole model, prior included, predicts the data.
evidence: Write the evidence as an integral over the parameters
Explain why a needlessly wide prior lowers the evidence
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why does the evidence penalise a model with an unnecessarily wide prior?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Gaussian-process hyperparameters from the data
topics.description: The length scale, amplitude and noise can be chosen by maximising the marginal likelihood or sampled hierarchically; the marginal likelihood balances fit against complexity.
evidence: Fit hyperparameters by marginal likelihood
Interpret its fit and complexity terms
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why does the marginal likelihood not simply prefer the wiggliest fit?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Smoothing priors are Gaussian, and flat in places
topics.description: A Laplacian smoothing penalty is a Gaussian prior with a singular precision matrix: patterns it does not penalise, such as constants or linear trends, are flat directions of the prior.
evidence: Identify the null space of a smoothing operator
Compare draws from a smoothing prior and a Gaussian process
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why can't you draw samples directly from a pure Laplacian smoothing prior?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Prior fields on a fault plane
topics.description: Gaussian-process and smoothing priors extend to two-dimensional slip on a fault surface, with length scales along strike and down dip.
evidence: Draw a 2-D Gaussian-process field
topics.assessmentPrompt: Should the along-strike and down-dip length scales be equal?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Two kinds of error: C_d and C_p
topics.description: C_d describes measurement noise; C_p describes prediction (model) error from an imperfect forward model. Both enter the likelihood through the misfit covariance C_χ = C_d + C_p.
evidence: Name a source of each kind of error
Explain why C_p is correlated across stations
topics.assessmentPrompt: An approximate elastic structure causes which kind of error?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Building C_p from sensitivities
topics.description: Linearise the predictions with respect to an uncertain structural parameter, multiply this sensitivity by the parameter's uncertainty, and form the covariance of the resulting prediction errors.
evidence: Compute a sensitivity by finite differences
Form C_p for one uncertain parameter
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why does C_p depend on the slip model itself?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: When C_χ = C_d + C_p is valid
topics.description: Adding the two covariances assumes zero-mean errors, noise independent of model error, a first-order Gaussian approximation, and a reasonable reference model.
evidence: List the four assumptions
Give a case that breaks one of them
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why must model error be independent of noise for the covariances to add?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: What leaving C_p out does
topics.description: Ignoring model error makes posteriors too narrow and often biased: credible regions miss the true value far more often than their nominal probability.
evidence: Run a coverage test with and without C_p
topics.assessmentPrompt: Your posteriors are narrow but often wrong in synthetic tests. What might be missing?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: A model error the slip cannot mimic
topics.description: When the model error's pattern looks unlike any slip prediction, it shows up as misfit and an inflated χ² rather than as biased slip.
evidence: Distinguish the two possible outcomes of a model error
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why can some model errors be seen in the residuals and others not?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: GNSS noise: white, flicker and random walk
topics.description: GNSS position series contain white noise plus time-correlated flicker and random-walk noise; the correlated parts make rate uncertainties much larger than white-noise formulas suggest.
evidence: Simulate the three noise types
Explain why the rate error depends on the series length
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why do white-noise rate uncertainties look optimistic?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Estimating noise: periodogram and maximum likelihood
topics.description: The slope of the power spectrum (the spectral index) identifies the noise type; maximum likelihood estimates the amplitudes, although random-walk amplitudes are hard to recover from short series.
evidence: Read a spectral index from a periodogram
Fit noise amplitudes by maximum likelihood
topics.assessmentPrompt: Which noise has a spectral index near −1?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: InSAR: covariograms of the atmosphere
topics.description: Atmospheric delays make InSAR errors spatially correlated; an empirical covariogram, fitted with an exponential model, gives a full data covariance.
evidence: Compute an empirical covariogram
Fit an exponential covariance model
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why are the errors of neighbouring InSAR pixels correlated?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Decimation and data weight
topics.description: Reducing millions of InSAR pixels to hundreds (uniform or quadtree sampling) changes how much weight the data set carries; with a diagonal C_d, more points mean more weight even when they share errors.
evidence: Compare uniform and quadtree decimation
Explain how decimation changes a data set's effective weight
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why can doubling the number of decimated points double InSAR's apparent influence?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Tsunami records: correlation, sampling and filtering
topics.description: Ocean-bottom pressure and tide-gauge records have temporally correlated noise; resampling and filtering change it, and must be applied consistently to the records, the predictions and the covariance.
evidence: Propagate a covariance through a filter
Explain why interpolation makes errors correlated
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why must the same filter be applied to the Green's functions as to the records?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: The effective number of independent data
topics.description: Correlated data carry less information than their count suggests; the effective number of independent data levels off once sampling is denser than the correlation length or time.
evidence: Compute the effective number of data for a correlated series
Explain why it depends on the quantity being estimated
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why does sampling a GNSS series every second instead of every day add little information about its rate?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: One noise scale per data set or a full covariance
topics.description: Scaling a diagonal C_d by one factor per data set fixes the overall size of the errors but not their correlation; only the full covariance gets both right.
evidence: Compare coverage with a diagonal, a scaled and a full C_d
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can fitting one noise scale for InSAR repair an ignored spatial correlation?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Which method for which shape
topics.description: Grid, Metropolis, NUTS, SMC, EnKI and EKF succeed and fail on different posterior shapes and budgets; the report card summarises these examples and implementations, not a general law.
evidence: Pick a method for a ridge, a banana, two modes and a funnel
Explain why a method's success on one shape need not transfer
topics.assessmentPrompt: Which of the course's methods recovers both modes of a two-island posterior?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Markov chains and stationary distributions
topics.description: A sequence in which each step depends only on the current state; designed well, it converges to a stationary distribution, the target posterior, whatever its starting point.
evidence: Explain the Markov property
Say what irreducibility and aperiodicity guarantee
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why does a well-designed chain forget its starting point?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: The Metropolis algorithm
topics.description: Propose a random jump; accept it with probability min(1, p(new)/p(old)); otherwise stay and count the old point again. The chain's points are samples from the posterior.
evidence: Run Metropolis by hand for three steps
Explain why a rejected proposal repeats the current point
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why must a rejected proposal be counted again?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Detailed balance and the Hastings correction
topics.description: Metropolis targets the right distribution because, at equilibrium, each move is as likely as its reverse (detailed balance); asymmetric proposals need the Hastings factor q(old | new) / q(new | old).
evidence: Write the Metropolis-Hastings acceptance ratio
Explain what goes wrong without the Hastings factor
topics.assessmentPrompt: A multiplicative proposal without the Hastings factor samples what instead of the target?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Step size and acceptance rate
topics.description: Tiny steps are almost always accepted but move slowly; huge steps are almost always rejected; a tuned step balances the two.
evidence: Tune a step size from the acceptance rate
Recognise too-small and too-large steps in a trace
topics.assessmentPrompt: An acceptance rate of 0.99 suggests what about the step size?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Autocorrelation and the ESS of a chain
topics.description: Successive samples of a chain are correlated; the autocorrelation time says how many steps make one effectively independent draw, and sets the effective sample size.
evidence: Compute an autocorrelation function
Estimate the effective sample size of a chain
topics.assessmentPrompt: A chain needs 50 steps per independent draw. What is the effective sample size of 10,000 draws?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Correlated targets and shaped proposals
topics.description: On a tilted ridge a round proposal must take tiny steps; proposals shaped like the posterior covariance move along the ridge.
evidence: Explain why trade-offs slow a random walk
Shape a proposal with a covariance estimate
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why does a round proposal crawl along a narrow ridge?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Why dimension hurts a random walk
topics.description: In many dimensions a random proposal almost always points away from the high-probability region, so the step must shrink and mixing slows dramatically.
evidence: Show the acceptance rate falling with dimension at a fixed step
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why does Metropolis struggle with hundreds of slip patches?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: JAX: grad, jit and vmap
topics.description: A NumPy-like library whose function transformations compute gradients automatically (grad), compile code (jit) and vectorise over an ensemble (vmap).
evidence: Take the gradient of a log posterior with jax.grad
Vectorise a forward model over an ensemble with vmap
topics.assessmentPrompt: What does jit change between a function's first call and its later calls?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Automatic differentiation
topics.description: Exact derivatives of a program built from the chain rule; reverse mode gives the whole gradient for about the cost of a few forward runs, whatever the number of parameters, while finite differences need one run per parameter.
evidence: Compare autodiff and finite differences in accuracy and cost
Explain why reverse mode suits many parameters and one objective
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why is reverse-mode autodiff the right choice for the gradient of one log posterior with 1,000 parameters?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: What 'differentiable' means
topics.description: A log posterior is differentiable where its slope exists; jumps, rounding, look-up tables and black-box executables break that.
evidence: Identify the steps of a forward model that are not differentiable
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why does rounding the predictions break a gradient sampler but not Metropolis?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Gradient samplers need a smooth log posterior
topics.description: On a piecewise-flat surface the gradient is zero almost everywhere, so a gradient sampler wanders and builds the longest trajectories it can, while derivative-free methods are unaffected.
evidence: Diagnose a non-differentiable posterior from a gradient sampler's behaviour
topics.assessmentPrompt: A gradient sampler hits its maximum trajectory length on every draw. What could be wrong?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Hard bounds and transforms in samplers
topics.description: A gradient sampler cannot step over a hard wall; transforming to an unbounded variable (log or logit) with its Jacobian keeps every step legal. NumPyro does this automatically.
evidence: Compare sampling a bounded parameter with a wall and with a transform
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why does a bounded prior cause trouble for a sampler that slides on the log posterior?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Black-box physics: where gradients come from
topics.description: When the forward model is an external program, gradients can come from finite differences, an adjoint, a differentiable reimplementation or a surrogate; otherwise use derivative-free methods.
evidence: List four sources of gradients for a black-box forward model
topics.assessmentPrompt: Your forward model is a compiled Fortran code. What are your options for gradients?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: The gradient of the log posterior as arrows
topics.description: At every point the gradient points uphill toward higher posterior probability, with a length set by the steepness.
evidence: Draw gradient arrows on a 2-D posterior
topics.assessmentPrompt: Where on a posterior is the gradient zero?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: An optimiser finds one point; a sampler explores
topics.description: Following the gradient uphill gives the MAP; sampling needs motion that also visits lower-probability regions in proportion to their probability.
evidence: Contrast gradient-ascent paths with sampler paths
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why does following the gradient alone not give a posterior?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
topics.description: Treat minus the log posterior as a landscape and the parameters as a frictionless puck: give it a random momentum, let it slide with the leapfrog integrator, and accept the end point with a Metropolis test. Long moves follow ridges and curves.
evidence: Explain the roles of position, momentum and energy
Run HMC on a banana-shaped posterior
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why can HMC move far along a curved ridge in one step?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Leapfrog steps, energy error and divergences
topics.description: The leapfrog integrator nearly conserves energy; a step too large for the local curvature makes the energy error explode, a divergence, which flags regions the sampler cannot explore.
evidence: Relate the step size to the energy error
Interpret divergent transitions
topics.assessmentPrompt: What does a cluster of divergences in a funnel's neck tell you?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: NUTS: the no-U-turn sampler
topics.description: HMC that builds each trajectory by doubling until it starts to turn back (a U-turn), so the path length need not be tuned; the default sampler in NumPyro.
evidence: Explain the U-turn criterion
Read the tree depth as a cost diagnostic
topics.assessmentPrompt: What does NUTS choose automatically that plain HMC needs you to set?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Automatic step-size tuning
topics.description: During warm-up NUTS adjusts its step size (dual averaging) toward a target acceptance probability.
evidence: Explain why warm-up draws are discarded
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why can't step-size adaptation continue during the sampling phase?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Centred and non-centred parameterisations
topics.description: Writing m = α·u with u standardised removes the funnel between a scale α and the parameters it controls; which form works better depends on how strongly the data constrain those parameters.
evidence: Rewrite a hierarchical model in non-centred form
Say when the centred form is preferable
topics.assessmentPrompt: With very informative data, which parameterisation tends to behave better?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: The mass matrix
topics.description: A matrix that rescales and rotates the landscape for HMC; estimated from warm-up draws (diagonal or dense), it makes a tilted ridge look round.
evidence: Explain the difference between a diagonal and a dense mass matrix
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why does a dense mass matrix help on a strongly correlated posterior?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Warm-up (burn-in)
topics.description: The early part of a chain, which still remembers its starting point (and, for NUTS, is adapting its tuning); it is discarded.
evidence: Identify warm-up in a trace plot
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why discard the first part of a chain?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: R-hat
topics.description: Compares the spread between several chains with the spread within each; values near 1 (below about 1.01) mean the chains agree, which does not prove they are right.
evidence: Compute split R-hat for four chains
Explain why R-hat needs several chains
topics.assessmentPrompt: Four chains all stuck in the same wrong mode: what is R-hat?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Reading trace plots
topics.description: Plots of each chain's values against iteration reveal good mixing, sticky chains, drift and chains stuck in different modes.
evidence: Classify five trace-plot patterns
topics.assessmentPrompt: What does a trace that wanders slowly without settling suggest?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Chain ranges are a symptom, not a test
topics.description: Disjoint ranges per chain can come from short chains on one connected ridge, and overlapping ranges can hide separate modes in another coordinate; they prompt a closer look, not a verdict.
evidence: Give a counterexample in each direction
topics.assessmentPrompt: Chains have disjoint ranges after 100 draws. Is the posterior multimodal?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: R-hat = 1 does not mean correct
topics.description: Chains can agree with each other and all miss part of the posterior, such as a second mode none of them found; R-hat checks agreement, not correctness.
evidence: Construct an example with R-hat near 1 and a missed mode
topics.assessmentPrompt: How could you discover a mode that all chains missed?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Per-chain potential energy
topics.description: Comparing each chain's potential energy (minus the log posterior) quickly shows a chain stuck in a different region.
evidence: Print and compare per-chain energies
topics.assessmentPrompt: One chain's mean energy is far above the others. What does that suggest?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Monte Carlo standard error of what you report
topics.description: Every number reported from a sampler (a mean, a quantile) has its own Monte Carlo error, estimated from the bulk or tail effective sample size; report it beside the posterior spread.
evidence: Compute the MCSE of a posterior mean and of a 5 % quantile
Distinguish posterior spread from Monte Carlo error
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why is the Monte Carlo error of a tail quantile larger than that of the mean?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Three meanings of 'converged'
topics.description: A chain has converged when it has forgotten its start and samples the target; an optimiser when its steps stop; an ensemble Kalman method when its tempering parameter θ reaches one. These are different claims.
evidence: Use 'converged' precisely for each kind of method
topics.assessmentPrompt: An ensemble method reached θ = 1. Has it sampled the posterior?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Tempering
topics.description: Raising the likelihood to a power β between 0 (prior) and 1 (posterior) flattens the barriers between modes; the barrier height grows in proportion to β.
evidence: Plot a tempered posterior for several β
Explain why a low β lets a walker cross barriers
topics.assessmentPrompt: At β = 0, which distribution are you sampling?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Importance weights and resampling
topics.description: Moving particles from one tempered distribution to the next reweights each by the ratio of the two densities; resampling duplicates heavy particles and drops light ones.
evidence: Compute importance weights for a step in β
Explain what resampling does
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why do the weights become uneven when β jumps too far?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Sequential Monte Carlo
topics.description: A population of particles carried from the prior to the posterior through a sequence of tempered distributions, by reweighting, resampling and a few Metropolis moves per stage; CATMIP is an example.
evidence: Describe one SMC stage
Explain why SMC can find several modes
topics.assessmentPrompt: Which step of SMC lets particles move to new positions?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Adaptive tempering schedules
topics.description: Each step in β is chosen so the weights stay acceptably even, measured by their effective sample size or their coefficient of variation.
evidence: Choose the next β from a target weight ESS
topics.assessmentPrompt: What happens to the number of stages when the data are very informative?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Particle degeneracy
topics.description: When a step in β is too large, a few particles carry nearly all the weight and resampling copies them, losing diversity.
evidence: Recognise degeneracy from the weights' effective sample size
topics.assessmentPrompt: After a large jump in β, how many distinct particles survive resampling?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: What tempering fixes, and what it does not
topics.description: Tempering helps a population cross between separated modes; on a single ridge or banana it does not by itself beat a well-shaped proposal. The two address partly different difficulties and can be combined.
evidence: Compare SMC with Metropolis and NUTS chains on two islands
topics.assessmentPrompt: Would you use tempering for a single narrow ridge?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: The evidence as an SMC by-product
topics.description: The product of the average weights over all stages estimates the evidence (marginal likelihood), useful for comparing models.
evidence: Explain where SMC's evidence estimate comes from
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why does SMC give the evidence almost for free?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Variational inference and the ELBO
topics.description: Choose a simple family of distributions and fit its parameters by maximising the evidence lower bound (ELBO), which is the same as minimising a KL divergence from the family to the posterior.
evidence: Write the ELBO as an expected log density plus an entropy
Explain inference as optimisation
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why is the ELBO never above the log evidence?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: The reparameterisation trick
topics.description: Writing a random draw as a deterministic function of the family's parameters and standard noise lets the gradient of an average be estimated by averaging gradients.
evidence: Estimate the gradient of an expectation by reparameterisation
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why can't you differentiate through a call to a random-number generator directly?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Mean field, full rank and normalizing flows
topics.description: Mean-field families ignore correlations, full-rank Gaussians capture tilt but not curvature, and normalizing flows bend a simple distribution into complex shapes at a higher cost.
evidence: Predict how each family fits a ridge and a banana
topics.assessmentPrompt: Which family fails on a strongly correlated posterior?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Mode seeking and under-dispersion
topics.description: Reverse-KL variational fits tend to lock onto one mode and understate the spread, especially for mean-field families on correlated posteriors; a common tendency, not a law.
evidence: Measure the coverage of a variational fit against a reference posterior
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why does a mean-field fit often report error bars that are too small?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Variational inference on a ridge the data cannot resolve
topics.description: Where the data leave a trade-off ridge, the variational families tested covered little of it and gave no warning, while NUTS flagged trouble with divergences.
evidence: Compare variational inference and NUTS on a problem the data cannot resolve
topics.assessmentPrompt: Which diagnostic warns you when NUTS struggles, and does variational inference have one?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: The adjoint
topics.description: For a misfit computed from a model run, the adjoint gives the gradient with respect to all parameters with one extra backward solve; for a linear model it is the transpose Gᵀ applied without ever building G.
evidence: Explain the adjoint as Gᵀ applied implicitly
Pass the dot-product test
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why is one adjoint solve enough for the gradient of a single scalar misfit?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Deriving an adjoint by hand
topics.description: For a time-dependent model the adjoint runs backward in time, accumulating sensitivities; checking it against finite differences and autodiff catches mistakes.
evidence: Derive the adjoint of a small linear ODE
Verify it against finite differences
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why does the adjoint of a forward-in-time model run backward in time?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Discretise then differentiate, or the reverse
topics.description: The gradient of the discrete misfit (what an optimiser sees) and the discretised continuous adjoint differ by the discretisation error; the former matches finite differences of the computed misfit.
evidence: Explain which gradient matches finite differences
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why can a continuous adjoint disagree with finite differences?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: What a gradient costs
topics.description: Finite differences cost one run per parameter; forward mode one pass per parameter direction; reverse mode and adjoints a few runs whatever the number of parameters, paid for in memory.
evidence: Compare gradient costs as the number of parameters grows
topics.assessmentPrompt: With 40 parameters, which method's cost grows fastest?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: How gradients go wrong
topics.description: Gradients can be NaN while the forward run is fine (overflow in rejected solver steps), stiffness can make them expensive, and switches in the model (pinned patches) make them jump.
evidence: Diagnose a NaN gradient
Spot a switch that breaks differentiability
topics.assessmentPrompt: Your gradient is NaN but the forward run is fine. What could cause it?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Sequential Bayes
topics.description: Data can be absorbed one batch at a time: today's posterior becomes tomorrow's prior, and for a static linear-Gaussian problem the result equals using all the data at once.
evidence: Show that sequential and batch updates agree
Explain when they differ
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does the order in which independent data are absorbed change a linear-Gaussian posterior?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Predict, then update: process noise
topics.description: When the unknowns change in time, each step first predicts forward with a model plus process noise Q, widening the uncertainty, then updates with the new data. Q sets how fast the filter forgets.
evidence: Run predict and update steps for a random-walk state
Explain the effect of Q on tracking
topics.assessmentPrompt: What happens to a filter's response if Q is set to zero?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Filter or smoother
topics.description: A filter uses the data up to now; a smoother (RTS) also uses later data, giving better estimates of past states.
evidence: Compare filtered and smoothed estimates
topics.assessmentPrompt: To reconstruct a slip history after the fact, which one do you want?
