topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: The Network Inversion Filter
topics.description: A Kalman filter that estimates time-varying fault slip from GNSS time series, with the slip rate as an evolving state.
evidence: Describe the state and observation model of a Network Inversion Filter
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why model the slip rate as a random walk in a Network Inversion Filter?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: An ensemble carries the covariance
topics.description: A cloud of model samples (members) stands in for the mean and covariance; the Kalman update is computed from ensemble statistics instead of stored matrices.
evidence: Compute the gain from ensemble covariances
Explain why the ensemble size matters
topics.assessmentPrompt: With 20 members, what is the largest possible rank of the sample covariance?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Statistical linearisation: no derivatives needed
topics.description: The cross-covariance between members' parameters and their predictions acts as an average slope of the forward model, so no gradient is needed.
evidence: Compare an ensemble slope with a tangent slope
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why can ensemble methods use a black-box forward model?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: The ensemble Kalman filter (EnKF)
topics.description: Tracks a state that evolves in time with an ensemble: forecast each member, then update all members with the new data.
evidence: Run an EnKF on a slowly evolving state
topics.assessmentPrompt: What does the forecast step do to each member?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Classic EKI and ensemble collapse
topics.description: Applying the same data repeatedly at full weight makes the ensemble shrink toward a point: it behaves like an optimiser, not a sampler.
evidence: Show the ensemble spread shrinking with iterations
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why does reusing the data at full weight over-count it?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: EnKI: tempered ensemble Kalman inversion
topics.description: Assimilates the data in fractions Δθ that add up to one, like tempering; for linear-Gaussian problems a large ensemble reproduces the posterior, otherwise it gives a mean-and-covariance approximation.
evidence: Explain the θ schedule
State when EnKI reproduces the posterior
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why must the fractions Δθ add up to exactly one?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Nonlinear problems through a mean-and-covariance update
topics.description: Each member moves along directions set by ensemble statistics; on a curved posterior the cloud bends only partway, because the update uses means and covariances.
evidence: Compare an EnKI cloud with a reference banana posterior
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why can't one EnKI update follow the curve of a banana?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Capping Δθ
topics.description: Limiting the tempering step while the ensemble is still wide avoids large linearised jumps on strongly nonlinear problems.
evidence: Explain when a cap on Δθ matters
topics.assessmentPrompt: When does capping Δθ change the result?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: θ as a health monitor
topics.description: A θ that crawls while the misfit stays high is an alarm with several possible causes: strong nonlinearity, too small an ensemble, model error, or a bug.
evidence: List the causes of a stalled θ
topics.assessmentPrompt: θ has crept to 0.3 after many iterations. What do you check first?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: The subspace property
topics.description: Without localization, every EnKI member stays a combination of the initial members, so the answer lives in their span; with fewer members than unknowns the result depends on the random seed.
evidence: Explain why the update cannot leave the initial span
Run two seeds and compare them
topics.assessmentPrompt: With 20 members for 30 unknowns, why do two seeds give different answers?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Measuring the degree of nonlinearity
topics.description: The RMS of what the forward model's tangent, or an ensemble's straight-line fit judged on members it was not fitted to, misses over the region of uncertainty, in units of the data noise.
evidence: Compute a tangent-based nonlinearity index
Explain why an ensemble fit must be judged on held-out members
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why can an in-sample straight-line fit report zero nonlinearity with fewer members than parameters?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: The extended Kalman filter
topics.description: Applies the Kalman update to the forward model's tangent at the current estimate; the iterated EKF re-linearises (Gauss-Newton) and, when it converges, stops at a local MAP. Its covariance is the Gauss-Newton approximation, not the full Laplace covariance.
evidence: Run the classic and iterated EKF on a curved problem
Explain the difference between the Gauss-Newton and Laplace covariances
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why does the EKF covariance differ from the Laplace covariance when the residuals are large?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Kalman methods degrade with nonlinearity; samplers do not
topics.description: As the nonlinearity index grows, EKF and EnKI draws fall increasingly outside the reference posterior, while NUTS, SMC and Metropolis keep the right coverage in these tests.
evidence: Read a coverage-against-nonlinearity plot
topics.assessmentPrompt: At what point would you switch from EnKI to a sampler?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Where you linearise matters
topics.description: A sequential EKF linearises each datum once, at the estimate available then; poor early linearisation points bias the result until the posterior narrows.
evidence: Compare a sequential EKF with an iterated EKF on a time series
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why can an EKF that absorbs data day by day be biased early on?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Sampling error and spurious correlation
topics.description: A small ensemble estimates covariances noisily: unrelated parameters show chance correlations, and the sample covariance has rank at most the number of members minus one.
evidence: Estimate the scatter of a sample correlation for 20 members
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why do 20 members report correlations between distant, unrelated patches?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Localization: tapering covariances
topics.description: Multiplying the sample covariance entry by entry by a taper (such as Gaspari-Cohn) that dies off with distance removes spurious long-range correlations and raises the rank.
evidence: Apply a Gaspari-Cohn taper
Explain where the taper enters the update
topics.assessmentPrompt: What does tapering do to the rank of a 20-member covariance?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Choosing the localization length
topics.description: A short taper removes noise but also real correlations (bias); a long one keeps the sampling noise (variance): the length is a bias-variance trade-off.
evidence: Choose a localization length from repeated runs
topics.assessmentPrompt: What happens if the localization length is much shorter than the true correlation length?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Inflation
topics.description: Multiplying the ensemble spread by a factor slightly above one counters the loss of spread in small ensembles; it fixes the spread, not the mean.
evidence: Apply multiplicative inflation
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can inflation correct a biased ensemble mean?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: The two-seed test
topics.description: Running the same inversion with two random seeds gives a computable gap that tracks the actual error of each run, without knowing the answer.
evidence: Run two seeds and compute their gap
topics.assessmentPrompt: Two seeds disagree by more than the posterior spread. What does that tell you?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Entropy
topics.description: The average surprise of an uncertain outcome; for discrete outcomes it is the average number of yes/no questions per outcome when many outcomes are coded together, in bits.
evidence: Compute the entropy of a biased coin
Explain why a single outcome still needs one question
topics.assessmentPrompt: A patch slips in 9 of 10 earthquakes. What is the entropy of 'did it slip?', in bits?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Differential entropy
topics.description: The continuous counterpart of entropy; for a Gaussian it grows with the logarithm of σ, so it measures spread and can be negative.
evidence: Compute the differential entropy of a Gaussian
Explain why only differences of differential entropy carry meaning
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can a differential entropy be negative?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Information gain
topics.description: The expected reduction in entropy from prior to posterior (the mutual information between parameters and data); for Gaussians it depends on the ratio of prior to posterior spread.
evidence: Compute the information gain of one Gaussian measurement
Use it to rank candidate stations
topics.assessmentPrompt: Where would a new station teach the most about deep slip?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Maximum entropy
topics.description: Among the distributions consistent with what you know (bounds, a mean, a variance), the one with maximum entropy assumes nothing more: uniform, exponential or Gaussian.
evidence: Name the maximum-entropy distribution for a known mean and variance
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you know only the mean and variance of an error, which distribution adds no further assumption?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: KL divergence
topics.description: A measure of how different one distribution is from another: the expected log ratio of their densities. It is never negative and is zero only when the two agree.
evidence: Compute the KL divergence between two Gaussians
Explain Gibbs' inequality in words
topics.assessmentPrompt: Is the KL divergence a distance?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: The asymmetry of KL
topics.description: KL(p‖q) and KL(q‖p) differ: one fitting direction covers all of p's mass, the other locks onto one mode. Which direction a method minimises decides its behaviour.
evidence: Fit one Gaussian to two peaks in both KL directions
topics.assessmentPrompt: Which KL direction does variational inference minimise?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: KL as the information one datum delivered
topics.description: The KL divergence from prior to posterior measures what one actual datum taught, including a shift of the mean; its average over possible data is the information gain.
evidence: Compute the KL from prior to posterior for two data values
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why can a surprising datum deliver more information than the average?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Maximum likelihood is minimum KL
topics.description: Maximising the likelihood finds the member of the model family closest, in KL, to the process that generated the data, even when the family is wrong.
evidence: Explain what maximum likelihood estimates when the model is misspecified
topics.assessmentPrompt: If the true noise is Laplace but you fit a Gaussian, what does maximum likelihood still find?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: KL as a measure of non-Gaussianity
topics.description: The KL divergence between a posterior and the Gaussian with the same mean and covariance measures how far the posterior is from Gaussian.
evidence: Compute a posterior's non-Gaussianity
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why is this number useful before choosing a Kalman-type method?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Hyperparameters
topics.description: Knobs of the prior or the noise model, such as a smoothing weight λ or a noise scale, that set how strongly the prior acts.
evidence: Name the hyperparameters of a smoothing inversion
Show how the answer changes with λ
topics.assessmentPrompt: What happens to a slip model as the smoothing weight goes to zero and to infinity?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: L-curve and generalised cross-validation
topics.description: Two ways to choose λ without probability: the corner of the misfit-roughness curve, and the λ that best predicts left-out data.
evidence: Locate an L-curve corner
Explain generalised cross-validation in words
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why is the L-curve corner a judgement rather than a probability statement?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: ABIC
topics.description: Akaike's Bayesian information criterion chooses hyperparameters by maximising the marginal likelihood of the linear-Gaussian problem: an empirical-Bayes choice.
evidence: Compute ABIC on a grid of λ
Relate ABIC to the evidence
topics.assessmentPrompt: Is ABIC a fully Bayesian treatment of λ?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: When the prior family is wrong, every criterion is wrong together
topics.description: Hyperparameter criteria pick the best member of an assumed family; if the family is wrong they can agree with each other and still miss.
evidence: Show several criteria agreeing on a wrong answer
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can several criteria agreeing on λ prove that the prior is right?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: AIC and BIC
topics.description: Criteria for comparing models with different numbers of parameters: AIC estimates a predictive KL loss, BIC approximates the log evidence; both trade the fit against the number of parameters.
evidence: Compute AIC and BIC for nested models
Explain their different penalty terms
topics.assessmentPrompt: Which criterion penalises extra parameters more as the data grow?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: The evidence depends on the prior width
topics.description: The evidence can be changed at will by widening the prior on a parameter the data constrain, so evidence comparisons depend on prior choices.
evidence: Show the evidence falling as a prior widens
topics.assessmentPrompt: Two models differ only in prior width. Can the evidence be made to prefer either?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Never rank weights with the weighted misfit
topics.description: A misfit computed with the weights being chosen always favours down-weighting the data; compare weighting choices with a measure that does not depend on the weights.
evidence: Explain the circularity
Choose a weight-free comparison
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why does a smaller weighted χ² not mean a better weighting?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Reporting the fit
topics.description: Report the WRMS and χ² of each data set, with a plot of data against predictions, rather than one combined number.
evidence: Compute the WRMS of each data set
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why can a good total χ² hide a badly fitted data set?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Hierarchical models
topics.description: Models with hyperparameters above the parameters (for example a smoothing scale and noise scales above the slip), all inferred together.
evidence: Draw the hierarchy of a slip inversion
topics.assessmentPrompt: Which quantities sit at the top of a hierarchical slip inversion?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Empirical Bayes or full hierarchical Bayes
topics.description: Empirical Bayes (as in ABIC) fixes the hyperparameters at their best values, a plug-in that ignores their uncertainty; full hierarchical Bayes samples them and carries that uncertainty into the parameters.
evidence: Compare a plug-in posterior with a hierarchical one
Explain when the difference matters
topics.assessmentPrompt: When the data barely constrain λ, which approach gives honest error bars?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Positivity breaks the ABIC formula
topics.description: With a positivity bound the posterior is a truncated Gaussian and the closed-form ABIC no longer equals the marginal likelihood; the normalisation inside the bound has to be included.
evidence: Explain why truncation changes the marginal likelihood
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why can't you use the linear ABIC formula for slip that must be positive?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Data weights: one noise scale per data set
topics.description: When data sets have unknown noise levels, a scale σ_k for each can be sampled with the parameters, setting their relative weights.
evidence: Set up a hierarchical model with one σ_k per data set
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why give each data set its own noise scale?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Estimated weights measure misfit
topics.description: An estimated σ_k reflects how far the model misses that data set, including model error from elsewhere, not only the quality of the instrument.
evidence: Show a weight absorbing an unmodelled ramp
topics.assessmentPrompt: A data set receives a large σ_k. Is its instrument bad?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Hyperpriors
topics.description: The prior on a hyperparameter is part of the model; flat or log-uniform hyperpriors can dominate the answer when the data are weak, so test the sensitivity.
evidence: Compare results under two hyperpriors
topics.assessmentPrompt: With weak data, what decides the smoothing scale?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: What 'objective' buys
topics.description: Estimating weights from the data removes hand-tuning, but the prior's form, the error model and the hyperpriors remain choices; objectivity is limited by what the data can resolve.
evidence: List the choices an 'objective' inversion still makes
topics.assessmentPrompt: If λ is estimated from the data, is the slip model free of assumptions?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Regularised (BR) and unregularised (BUR) Bayesian inversion
topics.description: Unregularised Bayesian inversion samples slip within bounds without a smoothing prior; regularised inversion adds a smoothing prior with an estimated weight. Each embodies different assumptions.
evidence: Describe the prior of each approach
Explain the role of the bounds in BUR
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does an unregularised Bayesian inversion have no prior?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Profile or marginal treatment of a hyperparameter
topics.description: Maximising over the slip for each hyperparameter value (a profile) differs from integrating the slip out (a marginal); the profile lacks a log-determinant term and can bias the hyperparameter.
evidence: Compute profile and marginal curves for a smoothing weight
topics.assessmentPrompt: Which term does a profile likelihood miss?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Does smoothing manufacture overlap?
topics.description: Smoothing can spread slip from one process into the region of another (for example coseismic slip and afterslip), creating apparent overlap; compare with unsmoothed or differently smoothed inversions.
evidence: Test an overlap with and without smoothing
topics.assessmentPrompt: How would you check that an overlap between slip modes is real?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Smoothing after sampling
topics.description: Averaging posterior samples over neighbouring patches after an unsmoothed inversion reduces noise without imposing smoothness before seeing the data (Jiang and Simons 2016).
evidence: Average samples over patches and recompute the uncertainty
topics.assessmentPrompt: What does averaging over patches do to the posterior standard deviation?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Model error in an unregularised inversion
topics.description: Without smoothing, structural model errors enter the slip directly; including C_p in C_χ = C_d + C_p is the remedy.
evidence: Compare an unregularised inversion with and without C_p
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why does an unregularised inversion need C_p more than a smoothed one does?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Is the evidence a fair judge?
topics.description: Evidence comparisons between smoothed and unsmoothed models depend on the prior widths and on correlations that simple estimators ignore.
evidence: List what an evidence comparison depends on
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can a wider bound alone change which model the evidence prefers?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Derived quantities: compute them per sample
topics.description: Compute any derived quantity (moment, peak slip, overlap, stress) for every posterior sample and summarise the results; computing it from the mean model is wrong for nonlinear quantities (Jensen's inequality).
evidence: Compute a derived quantity per sample
Explain Jensen's inequality with an example
topics.assessmentPrompt: Is the peak slip of the mean model the mean of the peak slips?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Point summaries and intervals
topics.description: Mean, median and MAP answer different questions; equal-tailed intervals cut the same probability from each tail, highest-density intervals are the narrowest, and for skewed posteriors they differ.
evidence: Compute equal-tailed and highest-density intervals
Choose a summary for a skewed posterior
topics.assessmentPrompt: Which interval can split into two pieces for a posterior with two peaks?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Marginal and joint statements
topics.description: Error bars for each parameter do not make a band for a whole profile; statements about several parameters together (differences, simultaneous bands) need the joint samples.
evidence: Compute the share of profiles that stay inside the per-patch bands
Compute a difference from joint samples
topics.assessmentPrompt: Two patches' 90 % intervals overlap. Can you still be confident that one slipped more?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Posterior predictive checks
topics.description: Simulate new data from posterior samples and compare them with the observed data through test statistics; failures reveal misspecification, although some wrong models pass.
evidence: Run a predictive check with a residual statistic
Explain why passing does not prove the model right
topics.assessmentPrompt: Your model passes every predictive check. Could it still be wrong?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Simulation-based calibration
topics.description: Draw parameters from the prior, simulate data, run the inference, and record the rank of the true value among the posterior draws; the ranks should be uniform. Passing means no departure was detected for those quantities, not that the code is correct.
evidence: Run simulation-based calibration for a simple pipeline
Explain why a data-dependent test quantity is needed
topics.assessmentPrompt: A pipeline that returns the prior passes the parameter-rank check. Which check catches it?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: LOO-CV and WAIC
topics.description: Compare models by how well they predict left-out data: leave-one-out cross-validation (exact or by importance sampling) and WAIC, which account for the prior through an effective number of parameters.
evidence: Compute LOO for nested models
Compare the result with AIC and BIC
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why can LOO prefer a model with more parameters than AIC does?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Reporting checklist
topics.description: Report which numbers were sampled and which derived, the fit of each data set with plots, the diagnostics with their Monte Carlo errors, and the prior and error-model choices.
evidence: Write a reporting checklist for an inversion
topics.assessmentPrompt: Which numbers in your results were sampled and which were derived?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: A flat prior: the data alone cannot decide
topics.description: With a flat prior on many patches, the null space leaves the posterior unbounded or wildly uncertain: the data alone do not determine the slip.
evidence: Show a flat-prior posterior failing
topics.assessmentPrompt: Why does 'let the data alone decide' fail for slip on many patches?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Positivity: slip cannot be negative
topics.description: Slip that cannot be negative is enforced through a bounded prior or a transform, which skews posteriors near zero.
evidence: Sample a positive slip model
topics.assessmentPrompt: How does positivity change the posterior of a patch with little slip?

topics.subject: Inverse problems and Bayesian inversion
topics.name: Every choice on one inversion
topics.description: One fault-slip problem solved with a flat prior, independent, smoothing and Gaussian-process priors, hierarchical scales, positivity and EnKI, showing how each choice changes the answer.
evidence: Compare slip and uncertainty across priors on one problem
Explain which choice dominates where
topics.assessmentPrompt: On a slip inversion, which choices move the deep slip the most?
